title: Two matching halves: symmetry in butterflies, leaves and faces

summary.text: A butterfly's left wings have the same shape and spots as her right wings, flipped over. When the two halves of a shape match like this, we say the shape has symmetry. Your child stands a small mirror on the middle line of a butterfly picture, a leaf, a spoon, a chappal and a photo of a face. With half of a butterfly and the mirror, the whole butterfly appears. With a chappal, the mirror makes a shape no chappal has. Half a face makes a face that looks like the person, but not quite, because real living halves nearly match but never exactly. Then your child makes symmetric art of their own.
summary.art: A girl standing a small hand mirror upright down the middle of a butterfly drawing. Half the drawing and the reflection make one whole butterfly.

intro.hook: Look at this butterfly. Is her left side the same as her right side?
intro.text: Show your child a butterfly, in a book, on a phone or at a balcony plant. Ask them to look at the wings on one side, then the other. What do they notice? Ask: if you could only see one side, could you draw the other side? Why do you think so? Don't answer yet. This unit finds out, with a mirror.
intro.art: A black and yellow butterfly resting on a curry leaf plant on a city balcony, wings spread flat, with a child's face peering close.

outcomes: By the end I can say that a shape has symmetry when its two halves match, like a butterfly's two sides.
By the end I can find the line of symmetry: the middle line where a shape folds into two matching halves.
By the end I can use a mirror to test whether a thing has two matching halves.
By the end I can say that butterflies, leaves and faces have two halves that nearly match, but never exactly.
By the end I can say why a butterfly needs two matching sides: so she can fly straight.
By the end I can make symmetric art, by copying one half onto the other side of a line.

terms.meaning: A shape has symmetry when its two halves match. One half is the same as the other, flipped over.
terms.example: A butterfly has symmetry. Her left wings match her right wings.
terms.art: A butterfly with her wings spread, the left wings and right wings the same shape and the same spots.

terms.meaning: The line of symmetry is the middle line of a shape. Fold the shape along this line, and the two halves match.
terms.example: On your face, the line of symmetry goes down the middle of your nose.
terms.art: A child's face with a dotted line drawn from the forehead, down the nose, to the chin.

terms.meaning: A mirror image is what you see in a mirror. It looks the same as the real thing, but flipped from side to side.
terms.example: Lift the hand nearest the window. Your mirror image also lifts the hand nearest the window.
terms.art: A girl lifting one hand in front of a mirror, and her mirror image lifting the hand on the same side.

terms.meaning: A half is one of two equal parts of a thing.
terms.example: Fold a chapati or a dosa in the middle, and you see two halves.
terms.art: A round dosa folded along the middle into two halves on a steel plate.

explanations.definition: A shape has symmetry when a line can cut it into two halves that match. The line is called the line of symmetry.
explanations.description: Look at a butterfly. Draw a line down the middle of her body. Her left wings and right wings have the same shape and the same spots. Fold her along that line, and the two sides would meet. That is symmetry. A leaf, a steel spoon, the letter A and your face have it. A chappal has none, because it is shaped for one foot.
examples: A butterfly: the line goes down her body.
A steel spoon: the line goes along it, from the tip to the end of the handle.
The letter A: the line goes straight down the middle.
A chappal and the letter F: no line works.
explanations.context: This card says what symmetry means. You looked for it in the Leaf Look and the Mirror Test.
explanations.art: Four pictures in a row: a butterfly, a spoon and the letter A, each with a dotted line down the middle, and a chappal with a question mark.

explanations.concept: Why a mirror shows the other half
explanations.definition: A mirror shows a thing flipped from side to side. So if you stand a mirror on the line of symmetry, the mirror shows the other half, and you see the whole shape.
explanations.description: In the Mirror Test, the mirror showed the paper half, flipped. For a butterfly, the flipped half looks just like her other half, so you saw a whole butterfly. For a chappal, the flipped half is different from the other half. So the mirror made a strange chappal that fits no foot.
examples: A mirror on a butterfly's middle line shows a whole butterfly.
A mirror on the letter A shows a whole A.
A mirror on the letter F shows a new shape, not an F.
explanations.context: This card says why the Mirror Test works. Read it after you have done the test.
explanations.art: A hand mirror standing upright on the middle of a letter A, showing a whole A, beside a mirror on a letter F showing a strange new shape.

explanations.concept: Why butterflies, fish and people have two matching sides
explanations.definition: Most animals that walk, swim or fly have a left side and a right side that nearly match. This helps them move straight ahead.
explanations.description: A butterfly flaps her left and right wings together. Wings of the same size push the same amount of air, so she can fly straight. If one wing were much smaller, she would fly crooked. A fish has a fin on each side. You have a leg on each side, so you can walk straight. We all have eyes and a nose at the front, where we are going.
examples: A butterfly has two wings on the left and two on the right.
A fish has a fin on each side of her body.
You have one leg on each side, so you can walk straight.
explanations.context: This card says why so many living beings have two matching sides.
explanations.art: A butterfly flying straight towards a hibiscus flower, a fish swimming with a fin on each side, and a child walking along a straight line on the floor.

explanations.definition: The two halves of a living being nearly match, but never exactly. Each half grows in its own place and has its own small differences.
explanations.description: In the Mirror Test, half a face and the mirror made a face that looked like the person, but not quite. That is because the two halves of a real face are not exactly the same. One eye may be a little higher, or one side of the smile a little wider. A folded leaf never meets perfectly at every edge. A butterfly may have a nick in one wing. Living beings are nearly even, each in their own way.
examples: Your face: each mirror face looked a little different from the real you.
A folded leaf: the two edges almost meet, but not all the way round.
Your heart sits a little to the left of the middle.
explanations.context: This card is about the surprise in the Mirror Test, when the mirror face did not quite look like the real person.
explanations.art: A photo of a smiling woman's face, and beside it two mirror-made faces, one a little wider and one a little narrower, both looking almost like her.

agreed.text: Most animals, including humans, have a left side and a right side that nearly match.
agreed.evidence: Look at a butterfly, a crow, a fish, a cat or a friend. Each has the same parts on both sides: wings, eyes, fins, legs or ears.

agreed.text: A mirror on the line of symmetry shows the whole shape.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can try it with a hand mirror on a leaf, a spoon or the letter A, and see the whole thing.

agreed.text: Living beings are never perfectly symmetric.
agreed.evidence: Folded leaves never match at every point. Mirror-made faces look a little different from the real face. The human heart sits a little to the left.

challenging.claim: A butterfly's two sides are exactly the same.
challenging.who: A common guess among children, and many grown-ups
challenging.for: From a little distance, the wings on each side look identical, with the same spots in the same places.
challenging.against: Look very closely, and there are tiny differences: a spot a little bigger, a scale rubbed off, or a nick where a bird pecked. The sides match nearly, never exactly.
challenging.context: This card asks whether a real butterfly is perfectly even.

challenging.claim: Only people make shapes with two matching halves.
challenging.who: Something people sometimes say, because a kolam or a temple is made so carefully
challenging.for: People do plan their kolams, rangolis and buildings to be even on both sides.
challenging.against: Butterflies, leaves, flowers, fish and our own bodies grow with matching halves too. Nobody draws them.
challenging.context: This card asks who makes symmetry: people, or living beings as well.

challenging.claim: The most symmetric faces are the most beautiful.
challenging.for: In some studies, many people picked the more symmetric face of two as the more attractive one.
challenging.against: Other studies find the effect is small, and that a perfectly mirrored face can look strange. What people find beautiful also changes from person to person and place to place.
challenging.context: This card asks whether more even faces really look more beautiful. Scientists still argue about it.

big_questions.q: Half a butterfly and a mirror showed you the whole butterfly. Was the other half already there, inside the half you had?
big_questions.hint: Where did the mirror get the other half from? What did it need to make it?

big_questions.q: Your two halves nearly match, but not exactly. Which half is the real you?
big_questions.hint: Is one half more you than the other? Or do you need both?

big_questions.q: Why do animals that move forward, like butterflies, fish and people, have a left side and a right side?
big_questions.hint: Think about flying, swimming or walking in a straight line. What would happen if one side were much bigger?

big_questions.q: Bees can learn to tell an even pattern from an uneven one. Is the symmetry in the butterfly, or in the eyes that look at her?
big_questions.hint: Would the butterfly still have matching wings if nobody looked? Who notices that they match?

story.title: Revathi's Half Butterfly
story.note: Made-up story. Lime butterflies really do lay their eggs on lemon and curry leaf plants, and their black wings with yellow spots really do match on both sides. Paati means grandmother in Tamil. Revathi, Kiran and Paati are made up.
text: Revathi was six. She lived on the third floor of a block of flats in Coimbatore. On the balcony, her Paati grew a curry leaf plant in a big clay pot.
One morning, a butterfly landed on the curry leaves. Her wings were black, with many yellow spots.
"A lime butterfly," whispered Paati. "She lays her eggs on lemon plants and curry leaf plants. Her caterpillars will eat the leaves."

Revathi ran for her drawing book and her crayons. She sat very still and began to draw. First she drew the butterfly's body, a long thin line down the middle of the page. Then she drew the two wings on the left side, with every yellow spot.
Just then, her little brother Kiran ran out onto the balcony. "Butterfly!" he shouted, and clapped.
The butterfly lifted into the air. She flew over the railing and away, past the water tank of the next building.
Revathi looked at her book. She had drawn only half a butterfly.
"Oh no," she said. "She has gone. Now I don't know what her other side looks like."
Kiran was four. He giggled. "Half a butterfly! Half a butterfly can't fly!"
Paati sat down on the step beside Revathi. "Look at your own face first," she said. She took out the little round mirror she used for her bindi. "What is on this side of your face?"
"One eye, one ear and one cheek," said Revathi.
"And on the other side?"
Revathi looked. "One eye, one ear and one cheek. The same again."
"The butterfly is like that too," said Paati. "Her right side has the same shape and the same spots as her left side, only flipped. So you already know her other side. It is in your drawing."
Revathi frowned. "How can it be in my drawing?"
Paati stood the mirror straight up on the line of the butterfly's body. "Look into the mirror, from the side of your drawing," she said.
Revathi bent her head and looked. In the mirror was the other half, with every yellow spot. Half on the paper and half in the mirror made one whole butterfly.
"She is whole!" said Revathi.

Then she had an idea. She took her crayons and drew the right wings on the paper, spot by spot. For every spot on the left, she drew a spot on the right, the same distance from the middle line. When she held the mirror up again, the drawing and the mirror matched.

Kiran wanted a whole butterfly too. So Revathi showed him. "You draw one side," she said, "and then copy it on the other side, like a mirror." Kiran's butterfly had very wobbly wings, but he was proud of it.
The next morning, the lime butterfly came back to the curry leaf plant. Revathi held her book up beside her, very quietly.
The spots matched her drawing. But Revathi saw something new. One back wing had a small piece missing from the edge, like a bite.
"Paati, her two sides are not the same any more," she whispered.

"Perhaps a bird pecked at her, or a thorn caught her wing," said Paati. "Even before that, her two sides were never exactly the same. Look closely at any living being. The two halves nearly match. Never exactly."
Revathi looked at the butterfly. Then she looked in the mirror at her own face, and smiled. Her smile went up a little more on one side.
"Nearly the same," she said. "Never exactly." And she drew a tiny piece missing from the back wing in her picture.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Revathi finds that she can know the butterfly's hidden side from the side she drew, because the two halves match. A mirror shows this at once. Then she sees that a real butterfly, and her own face, nearly match but never exactly.
ask: Revathi drew only half the butterfly. How did Paati's mirror show her the whole butterfly?
How did Revathi draw the other side by herself?
When the butterfly came back, what was different about her two sides?
Are the two sides of your face exactly the same? How could you check?
art: A black butterfly with yellow spots resting on a curry leaf plant in a clay pot on a city balcony, with a girl of six watching.
The girl drawing half a butterfly in her book, while a small boy runs onto the balcony clapping and the butterfly flies off.
A grandmother in a cotton saree standing a small round mirror on the girl's drawing, and the girl bending to look.
The girl's drawing with half on the paper and half in the mirror, making one whole butterfly.
The butterfly back on the curry leaves, one back wing with a small piece missing from the edge, and the girl holding up her book beside her.

experiments.title: The Mirror Test: can half a thing and a mirror make the whole?
experiments.context: In this experiment you stand a small mirror on the middle line of different things. You guess first, then look: does half the thing and the mirror make the whole thing again?
experiments.question: Can half of a thing and a mirror show you the whole thing? Which things work, and which do not?
experiments.predict: For each thing, guess first: will half of it and the mirror make the whole thing again? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Hold the mirror straight up every time, with its bottom edge on the line. When a thing does not work, try at least three different lines before you say no.

materials.item: a small flat mirror, such as a hand mirror or the mirror from a make-up compact
a picture of a butterfly with her wings spread flat, from a book, or drawn by a grown-up with both sides the same
a big flat leaf, such as a palak, money plant or hibiscus leaf
a steel spoon and a flat steel plate (thali)
one chappal and a door key
a sheet of paper with a big letter A and a big letter F written on it
a printed photo of a face looking straight ahead, such as a passport or school photo

experiments.safety: Use a mirror with a frame or plastic edges. If its glass edges are bare, a grown-up holds it.

schedule.what: Guess for each thing, test it with the mirror, try a face, then test three things of your own.

experiments.record: Make two heaps on the floor, 'whole again' and 'new shape'. A grown-up writes each thing's name on a scrap of paper to put in a heap. Then draw one thing from each heap, with a dotted line where you put the mirror.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Whole spoon, with the mirror along it
A new shape: a chappal for no foot
A new shape, not an F
Nearly the same face, but a bit different

setup.art: A table with a butterfly picture, a leaf, a steel spoon, a flat steel plate, a chappal, a key, a sheet with a big A and F, a passport photo and a small hand mirror.
setup.caption: 1. Put all the things on a table, with the mirror.

setup.art: A child's hand standing a small mirror straight up on the middle line of a butterfly picture, and the child looking in from one side to see one whole butterfly.
setup.caption: 2. Stand the mirror on the middle line. Look in from one side.

setup.art: Two heaps on the floor, one labelled 'whole again' with the butterfly, spoon, leaf and letter A, and one labelled 'new shape' with the chappal, key and letter F.
setup.caption: 3. Sort the things into two heaps.

flow.do: 1. Put all the things on the table. 2. Hold the mirror straight up on the middle line of the butterfly picture. 3. Show your child how to look in from one side.
flow.say: Look into the mirror from this side. You can see half the butterfly on the paper, and something in the mirror. What do you see?
flow.kid: Look into the mirror from one side. What do you see?
flow.parent: Hold the mirror straight up, with its bottom edge on the line. Your child may need to tip their head to see the paper half and the mirror together. For the spoon and plate, lay them flat and hold the mirror up on the middle line.

good: A whole butterfly!
Half is on the paper and half is in the mirror.

flow.do: 1. Point at each of the other things in turn. 2. Your child guesses: will half of it and the mirror make the whole thing? 3. A grown-up writes 'whole' or 'new shape' in the 'My guess' column. 4. Ask why.
flow.say: Now the leaf, the spoon, the plate, the chappal, the key and the letters. Will the mirror make each one whole again? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess for each thing. Will the mirror make it whole? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the chappal will work, or not work?
good: It will work, because it is long, like the butterfly.
It won't, because one side is bigger.
I don't know. Let's try.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Don't say what will happen. Write each guess down.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the mirror on each thing in turn, along the line they think is the middle. 2. If a line does not work, they try other lines. 3. They put each thing in a heap: 'whole again' or 'new shape'.
flow.say: Put the mirror on the spoon. Does it look like a whole spoon? Now try the chappal. Is there any line that makes a whole chappal?
flow.kid: Put the mirror on the spoon. Is it a whole spoon? Now try the chappal.

ask.q: What did the mirror make with the chappal?
good: A funny chappal that fits no foot.
A new shape, not a real chappal.
No line worked.

flow.parent: What you should see: the butterfly picture comes out whole. So do the spoon along its length, the plate and the letter A. The leaf comes out nearly whole. The chappal, the key and the letter F never do. The mirror makes a new shape instead.

flow.do: 1. Lay the face photo flat. 2. Ask your child to guess. 3. They stand the mirror down the middle of the nose. 4. They look at one half with the mirror. 5. They turn the mirror round and look from the other side, at the other half.
flow.say: Will half of this face and the mirror make the same face? What do you think, and why? Let's look. Now turn the mirror round and look at the other half.
flow.kid: Put the mirror down the middle of the nose. Is it the same face?

ask.q: Do the two mirror faces look like the real face?
good: Almost, but a bit different.
One looks rounder and one looks thinner.
It looks like a different person, a little.

flow.parent: This is the surprise. Each mirror face looks like the person, but not quite, and the two mirror faces differ from each other. The two halves of a real face are close, but never exactly the same.

flow.do: 1. Your child picks three more things from around the room, such as a fork, a bangle and a book. 2. For each one, they guess, then test it with the mirror on a line they choose. 3. They put each in a heap: 'whole again' or 'new shape'.
flow.say: Now you choose three things from this room. Guess first: will the mirror make each one whole again? Then test it, and tell me why you think it worked or not.
flow.kid: Pick three things. Guess. Test with the mirror. Put each in a heap.

ask.q: Which of your things came out whole, and why?
good: The bangle, because it is round and the same all round.
The book, because the two sides are the same.
The fork, along its length, but not across.

flow.parent: Any ordinary object will do. Round things and things with a clear middle usually come out whole. Things with a handle or a pattern on one side only usually do not. Let your child try several lines before they say no.

flow.do: 1. Look at the two heaps together. 2. Ask your child what they found, and what they saw that shows it. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: What did you find out? Which things did the mirror make whole? What did you see that tells you so?
flow.kid: What did you find? Which things came out whole?
flow.parent: A good answer has two parts. A claim: 'Things with two matching halves came out whole.' Evidence: 'The butterfly and the A did, but the chappal and the F made new shapes.'

check.q: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 1, stands a mirror on the middle of a letter F. What does she see?
options: A new shape that is not an F
check.why: The letter F has no line of symmetry. Its two halves don't match, so the mirror makes a new shape.

activities.title: Leaf Look: run a finger down the middle
activities.context: This is a short noticing activity, before anyone explains anything. You look closely at a leaf, find the line down the middle, and fold it gently.

materials.item: 2 or 3 fresh leaves, such as a palak leaf, a tulsi leaf, a money plant leaf or a curry leaf

schedule.what: Look at a leaf, find the middle vein, fold the leaf and compare the halves.

activities.record: Draw one leaf. Draw the middle vein as a line. Colour the two halves in two colours.

setup.art: A child's finger running down the thick middle vein of a green palak leaf, from the stalk to the tip.
setup.caption: 1. Run a finger down the middle vein.

setup.art: The same leaf gently folded along the middle vein, with the two edges almost meeting.
setup.caption: 2. Fold the leaf gently. Do the edges meet?

flow.do: 1. Give your child a leaf. 2. Ask them to find the thick line down the middle and run a finger along it, from the stalk to the tip.
flow.say: Look at this leaf. Can you find a line down the middle? Run your finger along it. What do you notice about the two sides?
flow.kid: Find the line down the middle of the leaf. Run your finger along it.
flow.parent: The thick line is the middle vein. It carries water into the leaf. Just let your child look and say what they notice.

flow.do: 1. Your child gently folds the leaf along the middle vein. 2. They look at the edges. 3. They do the same with a second leaf.
flow.say: Fold the leaf gently along that line. Do the two edges meet all the way round? Now try another leaf.
flow.kid: Fold the leaf along the line. Do the edges meet?

good: Nearly. The tip matches, but one side sticks out.
Yes, almost.
This leaf matches better than that one.

flow.parent: Most leaves fold into halves that nearly match, but the edges never meet perfectly. Fold gently, so the leaf does not break.

flow.do: 1. Look at the folded leaves together. 2. Ask the check question.
flow.say: So, is the left half of a leaf the same as the right half? Why might they be a little different?
flow.kid: Are the two halves the same? Why might they be a little different?

check.q: Kavya, a girl in Class 1, folds a tulsi leaf along the middle vein. What does she see?
check.why: A leaf grows one half on each side of the middle vein. The halves nearly match, but never perfectly.

activities.title: Dal Butterfly: build the other half
activities.context: In this art activity you make a butterfly from grains and dals on a drawn outline. One person makes a pattern on one side. The other copies it on the other side, like a mirror.

materials.item: a sheet of paper with a big butterfly outline drawn by a grown-up, with a line down the middle
a handful each of 3 or 4 kinds of grain or dal, such as rajma, chana, moong and rice
a small hand mirror, to check at the end

schedule.what: Make a grain pattern on one side, copy it on the other side, then swap.

activities.record: Draw your Dal Butterfly before you put the grains away, or take a photo.

setup.art: A butterfly outline on paper with a line down the middle, and a grown-up's hand placing three red rajma beans on the left top wing.
setup.caption: 1. One person puts grains on one side.

setup.art: A child placing three rajma beans on the right top wing in the same places, so the two sides match.
setup.caption: 2. The other person copies them on the other side.

flow.do: 1. Put the butterfly outline on the floor. 2. You place a pattern of grains on the left wings only. For example, 3 rajma near the top and a ring of moong lower down.
flow.say: I will make a pattern on this side only. Watch carefully. Your job is to make the other side match.
flow.kid: Watch the grains go on one side. Your job is to match them.
flow.parent: Keep the first pattern small: about 8 to 10 grains. Put some near the middle line and some far from it.

flow.do: 1. Your child copies the pattern on the right wings, grain by grain. 2. Remind them to put each grain the same distance from the middle line.
flow.say: For every grain on my side, put one on your side. Is it the same distance from the middle line? Is it the same kind of grain?
flow.kid: Copy each grain on your side. Same kind. Same distance from the line.

ask.q: How did you know where to put this one?
good: It is next to the line, like yours.
It is at the top, far from the line, like yours.

flow.parent: Children often copy the order of grains but not the distance from the line. If the butterfly looks lopsided, ask them to look at the distance.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands the mirror on the middle line to check. 2. Swap jobs. Your child makes a pattern, and you copy it, with one grain in the wrong place on purpose. 3. Your child finds the mistake.
flow.say: Let's check with the mirror. Now you make a pattern, and I will copy it. Can you find the grain I put in the wrong place?
flow.kid: Check with the mirror. Now you make a pattern. Find the grain in the wrong place.

check.q: Fathima, a girl in Class 1, puts 2 chana next to the middle line on the left wing. Where should she put 2 chana on the right wing, to match?
options: Far out at the edge of the wing
check.why: In a symmetric pattern, each grain on one side has a matching grain on the other side, the same distance from the middle line.

activities.safety: A grown-up watches, so that no grain goes into a mouth, nose or ear. Keep the grains away from any small child.

activities.title: Rub-and-Copy Art: fold, rub, and the other half appears
activities.context: In this art activity you draw half a picture next to a fold, then rub it onto the other half of the paper. The copy comes out flipped, like a mirror image.

materials.item: a sheet of plain paper, such as a page from a notebook
a soft, dark pencil, or a wax crayon
a steel spoon or a coin, for rubbing

schedule.what: Draw half a picture, fold the paper, rub, open it, then colour both halves to match.

activities.record: Colour both halves of your picture the same, and stick it on the wall.

setup.art: A sheet of paper folded in half and opened, with half a butterfly drawn in thick dark pencil on one side, right against the fold.
setup.caption: 1. Draw half a picture next to the fold, pressing hard.

setup.art: The paper folded shut with the drawing inside, and a child rubbing hard over it with the back of a steel spoon.
setup.caption: 2. Fold it shut and rub hard with a spoon.

setup.art: The paper opened to show a whole butterfly: the dark pencil half and a fainter copy on the other side, flipped.
setup.caption: 3. Open it. The other half has appeared.

flow.do: 1. Fold the paper in half and open it again. 2. Your child draws half a butterfly, half a flower or half a face on one side, right against the fold. 3. They press hard and go over the lines twice.
flow.say: Draw half a butterfly, right next to the fold. Press hard, and go over every line twice. What do you think will happen on the other side?
flow.kid: Draw half a picture next to the fold. Press hard. Go over the lines twice.
flow.parent: Thick, dark lines copy best. A soft pencil or a wax crayon works better than a light pencil.

flow.do: 1. Fold the paper shut, with the drawing inside. 2. Your child rubs hard all over the drawing with the back of a spoon or the edge of a coin. 3. Open the paper.
flow.say: Fold it shut. Rub hard all over, with the back of the spoon. Now open it. What do you see on the other side?
flow.kid: Fold it shut. Rub hard with the spoon. Now open it!

ask.q: What appeared on the other side?
good: The other half!
A copy, but it faces the other way.
A whole butterfly.

flow.parent: The copy is fainter, and it is flipped, like a mirror image. If it is too faint, go over the lines with the pencil.

flow.do: 1. Your child goes over the faint copy with the pencil. 2. They colour both halves the same. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Go over the faint lines. Now colour both halves the same. Is your picture symmetric? Where is its line of symmetry?
flow.kid: Go over the faint lines. Colour both halves the same.

check.q: Mrunal, a girl in Class 1, rubbed her folded drawing and opened it. Where is the line of symmetry of her picture?
options: Along the top edge of the paper
check.why: The copy is made by folding, so the two halves meet at the fold. The fold is the line of symmetry.

games.title: Mirror Moves: copy me like a mirror
games.players: 2 players, facing each other. A grown-up can be one of them. With 4 players, play as two pairs at the same time.
games.context: This is a moving game. One player is the leader and moves slowly. The other player is the mirror and copies every move at the same time.

printables.title: 10 move cards
items: Lift one arm up high, slowly.
Touch your nose with one finger.
Make butterfly wings with both arms.
Put both hands on your head.
Make a big smile, then a sad face.
Step one foot out to the side.

rules: Stand facing each other, about one big step apart.
The leader picks a move card and does the move very slowly.
The mirror copies at the same time, on the same side as a real mirror would. If the leader lifts the arm on the window side, the mirror lifts the arm on the window side too.
After 5 cards, swap: the mirror becomes the leader.
With 4 players, each pair uses its own 5 cards at a time, then the pairs swap piles. The game ends when all 10 cards are used. There is no winner. You both do well if you moved like one person.

setup.art: A mother and a girl standing face to face in a living room, about one step apart, with a small pile of move cards on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Stand facing each other.

setup.art: The mother slowly lifting the arm nearest the window, and the girl lifting her own arm nearest the window, like a mirror image.
setup.caption: 2. The leader moves slowly. The mirror copies on the same side.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the move cards and put them in a pile. 2. Stand facing each other. 3. Stand together in front of a real mirror first, and lift one arm.
flow.say: Look in the mirror. When I lift the hand near the window, which hand does my mirror image lift? Now you will be my mirror.
flow.kid: Lift a hand at the mirror. Which hand does your mirror image lift?
flow.parent: In a real mirror, if you lift the hand nearest the window, your image lifts the hand nearest the window too. So when two people face each other, the mirror person lifts their other hand (left for right).

flow.do: 1. Take turns to be the leader, 5 cards each. 2. The leader does each move slowly. 3. The other player copies like a mirror.
flow.say: I am the leader. Copy me like a mirror, at the same time. Ready? Slowly now.
flow.kid: Copy the leader like a mirror. Same side. Same time.

ask.q: How did you know which arm to lift?
good: I lifted the arm on the same side as yours.
Like the mirror: the window side.

flow.parent: Children often lift the same hand as the leader, which is the opposite side. Point to the window or the door to help them use the same side.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: If I lift the arm on the window side, which arm do you lift as my mirror? What did our two bodies make together?
flow.kid: When you were a mirror, what did you two make together?

check.q: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 1, is the leader. She lifts the arm on the window side. Her friend is the mirror, facing her. Which arm does the friend lift?
options: The arm on the window side
The arm on the door side
check.why: A mirror copies on the same side. So the mirror lifts the arm on the window side too. Together, the two of them make one symmetric shape.

games.title: Two Halves or Not? Run to a side
games.players: 2 to 5 players. Take turns to be the reader. The reader holds the card and does not run.
games.context: This is a running game. The reader reads a card. Everyone else runs to the 'two halves' wall if the thing has matching halves, or to the 'no' wall if it does not.

items.b: Two halves. Her left wings match her right wings.
No. Each chappal is shaped for one foot.
No. Your thumb is on one side only.
Nearly two halves, one on each side of the middle vein.

rules: Choose one wall for 'Two halves' and one wall for 'No'.
The reader reads the front of a card out loud. Everyone else runs to the wall they choose.
The reader reads the back of the card. Everyone at the right wall gets a point.
For cards whose back says 'Nearly', a player at the 'Two halves' wall gets a point, and so does a player who stands in the middle and says why.
After each card, the next player becomes the reader. With 2 players, you swap after every card.
Play until all 12 cards are read. The most points wins. If points are level, you both win.

setup.art: Two walls of a room with paper signs, one showing a butterfly and the words 'Two halves', the other showing a chappal and the word 'No'.
setup.caption: 1. Put up a sign on each wall.

setup.art: A grown-up reading a card while a girl runs towards the 'Two halves' wall.
setup.caption: 2. Hear the card, then run to a wall.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Make two signs and put them on two walls. 3. Choose who reads first. 4. Explain the rules.
flow.say: The reader reads a thing. If it has two matching halves, run to this wall. If not, run to that wall.
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Two halves? Run to this wall. No? Run to that wall.

flow.do: Read the cards one by one. Read the back after everyone has run. Swap the reader after every card.
flow.say: A chappal! Two halves or not? Run! Now, why did you choose that wall?
flow.kid: Run to a wall. Then say why you chose it.

ask.q: Why did you run to that wall?
good: The mirror made a funny chappal.
A butterfly's wings match.
My face nearly matches, so I went in the middle!

flow.parent: If your child is not sure, let them fetch the real thing and try the mirror. The mirror is the real answer.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Which card was the hardest to choose? Why?
flow.kid: Which card was hardest? Why?

check.q: The card says 'Your face'. The back says 'Nearly two halves, never exactly'. Why does it say 'nearly'?
options: The two sides of a face are close but never exactly the same
check.why: In the Mirror Test, the mirror face looked like the person, but not quite. Faces nearly match, never exactly.

projects.title: My Leaf Rubbing Book: one leaf a day
projects.context: In this project you make a small book of leaf rubbings. Each day you rub one leaf with a crayon, draw its line of symmetry, and look at how well the two halves match.

materials.item: 3 sheets of paper, folded in half and tied with thread into a little book
wax crayons, with the paper wrappers peeled off
a fresh leaf each day, from a potted plant or the kitchen, such as palak, tulsi, money plant or curry leaves

schedule.what: Make the book. Rub the first leaf and draw its middle line.
Rub a different leaf and draw its middle line.
Rub a third leaf, then compare all three.

projects.record: The finished book, with one leaf rubbing on each page and a line of symmetry drawn on each.

setup.art: A leaf lying under a sheet of paper, bumpy side up, and a child rubbing over it with the side of a green crayon so the shape and veins appear.
setup.caption: 1. Put the leaf under the paper. Rub with the side of a crayon.

setup.art: A leaf rubbing in a little book, with a pencil line drawn down the middle vein and the two halves coloured in two colours.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the middle line. Do the halves match?

flow.do: 1. A grown-up folds the sheets and ties them with thread to make the book. 2. Put the leaf under the first page, bumpy side up. 3. Your child rubs over it with the side of a crayon until the shape and veins show. 4. They draw a line down the middle vein.
flow.say: Rub gently with the side of the crayon. Watch the leaf appear! Now draw a line down the middle. Do the two halves look the same?
flow.kid: Rub with the side of the crayon. Watch the leaf appear. Draw a line down the middle.
flow.parent: The back of a leaf has bumpier veins, so it gives a clearer rubbing. Hold the leaf still with one hand.

flow.do: Your child rubs a different kind of leaf on the next page and draws its middle line.
flow.say: Here is a different leaf. Before you rub, guess: will its two halves match better or worse than yesterday's leaf? Why?
flow.kid: Rub today's leaf. Draw its middle line. Is it more even than yesterday's?

flow.do: 1. Your child rubs a third leaf. 2. Look through the whole book together. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Which of your three leaves has the halves that match best? Do any of them match exactly?
flow.kid: Rub one more leaf. Which leaf matches best?

check.q: Bornali, a girl in Class 1, draws a line down the middle vein of her leaf rubbing. What is this line called?
check.why: The middle vein is the line where the leaf folds into two halves that nearly match. That line is its line of symmetry.

challenges.title: The Balancing Butterfly
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. You cut a paper butterfly and try to balance her on a pencil, along her middle line.
challenges.problem: Nila, a girl in Class 1, wants to make a paper butterfly that balances on a pencil laid along her body. When does the butterfly balance, and when does she tip over?
constraints: Use one piece of card or thick paper.
The pencil must lie under the butterfly's middle line, from head to tail.
materials: a piece of thin card, such as an old greeting card or the side of a box
a pencil that does not roll, with flat sides (or a round pencil taped to the table at both ends)
general: Fold the card in half and cut half a butterfly against the fold. When you open it, both wings are the same.
Bend the wings down a little, like a tent. A butterfly with matching wings balances on the pencil along her middle line.
If one side is heavier, she tips towards that side.
creative: Add a paper clip to one wing, and watch her tip. Then add one to the other wing in the same place.
Cut a bit off one wing on purpose. What must you do to the other wing to make her balance again?
Bend the wings down more, like a tent. Does she balance more easily?
challenges.your_turn: Make your butterfly balance with two paper clips on her. Where did you put them? Why does that work?

setup.art: A folded piece of card with half a butterfly drawn against the fold, and a child cutting along the line with scissors.
setup.caption: 1. Fold the card. Cut half a butterfly against the fold.

setup.art: The opened card butterfly resting on a pencil that lies along her middle line, her wings bent down a little like a tent, balancing.
setup.caption: 2. Rest her on a pencil, along her middle line.

setup.art: The same butterfly tipping over to one side, with a paper clip on one wing only.
setup.caption: 3. Add a clip to one wing. What happens?

flow.do: 1. Read the problem to your child. 2. Fold the card in half. 3. Your child draws half a butterfly against the fold and cuts along the line. 4. Open the card.
flow.say: We will make a butterfly that balances on a pencil. Let's fold the card and cut half a butterfly against the fold. What will we have when we open it?
flow.kid: Fold the card. Draw half a butterfly by the fold. Cut it out. Open it.
flow.parent: Help with the cutting if the card is thick. Keep the fold uncut, or the wings will come apart.

flow.do: 1. Lay the pencil on the table. If it is round, tape both ends to the table. 2. Your child bends the wings down a little, like a tent. 3. They rest the butterfly on the pencil, with the fold along the pencil. 4. Then they add a paper clip to one wing, and then to the other.
flow.say: Put her on the pencil, along the fold. Does she balance? Now put a paper clip on one wing. What do you think will happen? Why?
flow.kid: Put her on the pencil along the fold. Does she balance? Now add a clip to one wing.

good: One side was heavier.
The clip was only on one wing.
Her two sides were not the same any more.

flow.parent: With both wings the same, she balances. With a clip on one side only, she tips down on that side. A clip on each wing, in the same place, balances her again.

flow.do: 1. Your child makes the butterfly balance with two clips. 2. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Make her balance with two clips. Where did you put them? Why does that work?
flow.kid: Make her balance with two clips. Where did you put them?

check.q: Gurpreet, a girl in Class 1, puts a paper clip on the left wing of her paper butterfly, and the butterfly tips over. What can Gurpreet do?
options: Put a clip on the right wing in the same place
Put another clip on the left wing
check.why: A clip on each wing in the same place makes the two sides match again. Then the butterfly balances along her middle line.

items.p: A grown-up reads the choices. Draw a line from each thing to its line of symmetry.
pairs: Down her body, from head to tail
Down the middle of the nose
Along it, from the tip to the end of the handle
items.why: Each line cuts the thing into two halves that nearly match. A strong answer matches all four and can show each line with a finger on the real thing.
items.art: A butterfly, a leaf, a face and a spoon on the left, and four short descriptions of lines on the right.

items.p: Here is half a butterfly, next to a dotted line. Draw the other half, so the two sides match. Then colour both sides the same.
items.a: A whole butterfly, with the same wing shapes and spots on both sides of the dotted line.
items.why: A strong drawing puts each spot the same distance from the line on both sides, and uses the same colours.
items.art: Half a butterfly with three spots on her wings, drawn to the left of a dotted vertical line, with the right side blank.

items.p: Your left hand is a mirror image of your right hand.
items.why: True. Put your two hands palm to palm, and they match, flipped over. A mirror image is the same shape, turned from side to side.

items.p: Sort these into two heaps: two matching halves, or no matching halves.
items.why: In the Mirror Test, the A, the plate and the leaf came out whole. The F, the key and the chappal made new shapes.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: what happened when you stood the mirror on the chappal?
items.a: The mirror made a strange chappal that fits no foot. No line made the real chappal again.
items.why: A strong answer says what the child saw, and that the chappal's two halves do not match.

items.p: Priya and Farida are talking about the Mirror Test.

views.says: My face is symmetric. I have one eye and one ear on each side, and my nose is in the middle.
My face is not symmetric. When I put the mirror on my photo, the mirror face did not look like me.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other one has right.
items.a: A strong answer says both are partly right. Priya is right that a face has matching parts on each side. Farida is right that the halves are not exactly the same, because the mirror face looked a little different.
items.why: A face is nearly symmetric, never exactly. A child who picks either side and uses the Mirror Test as evidence is thinking well.

items.p: Three of these have two matching halves. Circle the one that does not.
items.why: No line cuts the letter F into two matching halves. The A, the butterfly and the plate each have a line of symmetry.

items.p: Draw your own face, looking in a mirror. Draw a line down the middle. Then draw one thing that is a little different on your two sides.
items.a: A face with a line down the nose, and one small difference marked, such as one eyebrow higher or a mole on one cheek.
items.why: A strong drawing shows matching parts on both sides and one real difference, because faces nearly match but never exactly.
items.art: An empty oval for a face, with a dotted line down the middle.

items.p: A butterfly has 3 legs on her left side and 3 legs on her right side. How many legs does she have in all?
items.why: Three on the left and three on the right make 6. The two sides match, so each side has the same number.

items.p: Sunita, a girl in Class 1, folds a paper in half and cuts a shape on the fold. She opens the paper. What does she see?
opts: A shape with two matching halves
items.why: The two halves were cut together, so they match. The fold becomes the line of symmetry.

items.p: Put the Mirror Test in order.
items: Sort the things into two heaps
Stand the mirror on the middle line
a: Stand the mirror on the middle line
Sort the things into two heaps
items.why: First we guess, so the test can tell us whether we were right. Then we try the mirror. Then we sort what we found.

items.p: Bornali, a girl in Class 1, stands a mirror on the middle line of a hibiscus flower. What does she see?
opts: Half a flower and an empty mirror
A new shape, not a flower
items.why: A hibiscus flower has a line through its centre that cuts it into two matching halves. So the mirror shows the other half, and she sees a whole flower.

items.p: Say whether each thing has two matching halves: yes, nearly or no. A grown-up writes your answers.
items.why: A strong answer says 'nearly' for the face, because the Mirror Test showed small differences. Flowers are living too, so 'nearly' is also a good answer for the hibiscus.
items.art: A hibiscus flower, a face, a door key and a steel spoon in a row, with an empty label under each.

items.p: Your heart sits right in the middle of your chest.
items.why: False. Your heart sits a little to the left of the middle. On the outside your two sides nearly match, but inside they are not the same.

items.p: Draw a kolam or a rangoli that is the same on both sides of a line. Check it with a mirror.
items.a: A pattern with a line down the middle, where each loop or dot on one side has a matching one on the other side.
items.why: A strong drawing puts each part the same distance from the line on both sides, so the mirror shows the same pattern.
items.art: A square of dots with a dotted line down the middle, for the child to draw on.

items.p: The middle line where a shape folds into two matching halves is called the line of ___.
items.why: The line of symmetry cuts a shape into two halves that match.

items.p: Tsering, a girl in Class 1, cuts a paper butterfly. One wing comes out much bigger than the other. She rests the butterfly on a pencil along her middle. What happens?
opts: She tips towards the bigger wing
items.why: The bigger wing is heavier. The two sides no longer match, so the butterfly tips towards the heavier side.

items.p: Divya, a girl aged 7, says: 'Only people make shapes with two matching halves.' Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: what would you tell Divya?
items.a: Butterflies, leaves and people grow two matching halves, and nobody draws them. People make symmetric kolams too, but they are not the only ones.
items.why: A strong answer uses something the child saw, such as the leaf or the butterfly, as evidence.

items.p: Draw a line from each piece of art to how you made its second half.
pairs: Copy each grain on the other side
Fold the paper and rub it
Fold the card and cut against the fold
items.why: All three ways make a second half that matches the first, flipped over. A strong answer can say which way made the most exact copy.

items.p: A paper kite with one side much bigger than the other flies straight.
items.why: False. The bigger side catches more wind and pulls the kite round. A kite needs two matching sides to fly straight.

quiz.p: A shape has symmetry. What does that mean?
quiz.why: Symmetry means the two halves of a shape match, like a butterfly's two sides.
A butterfly's left wings match her right wings. A chappal and most keys have no line that cuts them into matching halves.

quiz.p: Where is the line of symmetry on a butterfly?
opts: Down her body, from head to tail
Across her wings, from side to side
Round the edge of her wings
quiz.why: The line down her body has two wings on each side, and the two sides match.

quiz.p: Where is the line of symmetry on your face?
opts: Down the middle of your nose
quiz.why: A line down the middle of your nose has one eye, one ear and one cheek on each side.

quiz.p: Anjali, a girl in Class 1, stands a mirror on the middle vein of a leaf. She sees a whole leaf. What does that show?
quiz.why: The mirror shows the paper half flipped. A whole leaf appears only when the two halves match.

quiz.p: Are the two sides of your face exactly the same?
quiz.why: In the Mirror Test, the mirror face looked like the person, but not quite. Faces nearly match, never exactly.

quiz.p: Why does a butterfly need her two sides to match?
opts: So both sides push the same air, and she flies straight
So she stays warm at night
quiz.why: Matching wings push the same amount of air on each side. If one side were much smaller, she would fly crooked.

quiz.p: Mrunal draws half a flower next to a fold. She folds the paper shut and rubs it hard. What appears on the other half?
quiz.why: Rubbing copies the drawing onto the other half, flipped like a mirror image. Together the two halves make a whole flower.

quiz.p: What do we call the middle line where a shape folds into two matching halves?
quiz.why: Fold a shape along its line of symmetry, and the two halves match.

quiz.p: A bird pecked a small piece out of one wing of a butterfly. Do her two sides still nearly match?
opts: Yes, nearly, but now one side is a little different
quiz.why: Real butterflies nearly match, never exactly. A nick makes one small difference, and the rest of the wings still match.

videos.title: A butterfly coming out of her chrysalis and spreading her wings
videos.why: Shows a butterfly's four soft wings spreading out together, already matching, as in the story of how we found out.
videos.check: Find a real, not animated, clip of a butterfly coming out of a chrysalis, preferably an Indian species. Check that it does not say butterflies come from anything other than eggs and caterpillars.

videos.title: Butterfly wing scales up close
videos.why: Shows that a butterfly's spots are made of tiny coloured scales, and that the spots on both sides match.
videos.check: Find a short microscope clip of real butterfly wing scales. Check that it says plainly that the scales are part of the living butterfly and rub off easily.

videos.title: Drawing a kolam that is the same on both sides
videos.why: Shows a person drawing a symmetric kolam with rice flour, for the child to copy on paper.
videos.check: Find a clip of a woman drawing a real kolam at a doorstep, with no talking over it or with simple, accurate words. Check that the kolam has a clear line of symmetry.

applications: Kolam and rangoli makers draw one half, then copy it on the other side, so the pattern is even.
A tailor folds cloth in half and cuts both sides of a shirt or a blouse at once, so they match.
A kite must have two matching sides, or it spins instead of flying straight.
Builders of temples, mosques and palaces often make the two sides match, like the Taj Mahal in Agra.
Mehendi artists often draw the same pattern on both hands, flipped.

spotted.text: A kolam at a doorstep in Chennai in the month of Margazhi, the same on both sides.
spotted.art: A white rice-flour kolam outside a flat's door, with loops that match on both sides of a middle line.

spotted.text: A butterfly on a curry leaf or lemon plant on a balcony in Bengaluru, her wings spread flat.
spotted.art: A black and yellow lime butterfly on a potted lemon plant on a city balcony.

spotted.text: Paper kites at Uttarayan in Ahmedabad, each with two matching sides.
spotted.art: Many colourful diamond-shaped kites in a blue sky over rooftops, each with a line down the middle.

spotted.text: The Taj Mahal in Agra, where both sides match, though one tomb inside sits a little to one side.
spotted.art: The Taj Mahal reflected in its long pool, with matching towers on both sides.

spotted.text: Mehendi on a bride's two hands at a wedding in Hyderabad, the same pattern flipped.
spotted.art: Two hands held side by side with matching mehendi patterns, one the mirror image of the other.

open_questions.q: Why does the heart sit a little to the left in nearly every person?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found some of the first steps that tell a tiny growing baby which side is left. Why the body picks left, and not right, is still not fully understood.

open_questions.q: Why do many people find symmetric faces pleasing?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think a very even face is a sign of good health. Others think our eyes simply find even shapes easier to see. Studies do not agree yet.

open_questions.q: How does a growing butterfly put the same spots in the same places on both sides?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know some of the genes that make the spots. How the two sides keep so closely in step is still being studied.

ask_kids: Can you find something in this room with two matching halves?
Is your plate of food the same on both sides? Could you make it the same?
Which letters of your name have two matching halves?
If you saw only half a crow at the window, could you guess the other half?
Where does a fan, a door or a window have its line of symmetry?
What would happen if one of your legs were much longer than the other?

jokes.j: What did the left ear say to the right ear?
jokes.a: Hear, hear! We are a pair!

jokes.j: What did the left wing say to the right wing?
jokes.a: You look just like me, only backwards!

jokes.j: Why did the chappal not smile at the mirror?
jokes.a: Because the mirror made a chappal for no foot, and that was no laughing matter!

jokes.j: Why did half a dosa go to the mirror?
jokes.a: To feel like a whole dosa again!

jokes.j: Why did the butterfly's wings never argue?
jokes.a: Because each wing always agreed with the other side!

jokes.j: Why did the letter A get full marks?
jokes.a: Because both its halves gave the same answer!

jokes.j: Why did the letter F stay away from the mirror?
jokes.a: Because the mirror kept turning it into something else!

jokes.j: What did one eye say to the other eye?
jokes.a: Between you and me, something smells. It's the nose in the middle!

maths.problem: A butterfly has 4 wings. Half of them are on her left side. How many wings are on her left side?
maths.explain: Half of 4 is 2. Share the 4 wings into two equal groups, one for each side: 2 and 2.
maths.context: This is about a butterfly's two matching sides.
maths.why_maths: Halving shows how many parts are on each side of the line of symmetry.

maths.problem: In the Mirror Test, Nila, a girl in Class 1, tested 8 things. 5 came out whole again, and 3 made new shapes. Make a tally. Which heap was bigger, and by how many?
maths.answer: The 'whole again' heap was bigger, by 2.
maths.explain: Draw 5 strokes for 'whole again' and 3 strokes for 'new shape'. Match them up one by one. 2 strokes in the first heap have no partner, so it is bigger by 2.
maths.context: This is about the Mirror Test, where you sorted things into two heaps.
maths.why_maths: A tally shows at a glance which heap is bigger, so you can compare what you found.

maths.problem: In the Dal Butterfly, a girl puts 3 rajma and 4 moong on the left wings. Her partner must make the right wings match. How many grains does the partner need? How many grains are on the butterfly in all?
maths.answer: The partner needs 7 grains: 3 rajma and 4 moong. There are 14 grains in all.
maths.explain: To match, the right side needs the same as the left: 3 and 4 make 7. Both sides together are 7 and 7, which make 14.
maths.context: This is about the Dal Butterfly, where you copied grains from one side to the other.
maths.why_maths: A symmetric pattern always has the same number on each side, so the whole is double one side.

song.note: Topic-level song for Patterns and symmetry L1

links.why: For the parent: photos of butterflies found in India, to look at both sides of their wings with your child.

warmup.q: What do we call it when a shape's two halves match?
Where is the line of symmetry on your face?
warmup.a: Down the middle of your nose.

warmup.q: How many wings does a butterfly have?
Does a chappal have two matching halves?
warmup.a: No. Each chappal is shaped for one foot.

warmup.q: Are the two sides of your face exactly the same?
Why does a butterfly need matching wings?

roots.context: We have tested halves with a mirror and made matching art. Now we ask what two matching halves tell us about butterflies, leaves and ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: You stood a mirror on the middle line of a butterfly picture. Half the picture and the mirror showed the whole butterfly. On a chappal, the mirror made a shape no chappal has. So when two halves match, one half already tells you what the other half looks like.
deep_truth.habit: We think we must see the whole of a thing to know its shape. For a shape with two matching halves, one half is enough, because the other half repeats it, flipped over. The mirror shows this at once.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Mirror Test, half a butterfly, half a leaf and half a letter A, with the mirror, looked like the whole thing. Half a chappal and half a letter F made new shapes. Half a face made a face that looked like the person, but not quite.

three.who_am_i: You have a left side and a right side that nearly match. They grew together, at the same time, from one tiny cell.
three.what_is_life: A butterfly feels the air with both her antennae and tastes with her feet. Her matching wings carry her straight to the flowers she chooses.
three.what_is_this_world: Matching halves are all around us: in leaves, flowers, butterflies and faces, and in the kolams people draw.

roots.thread: A butterfly grows all four of her wings at the same time, inside her chrysalis, from the same instructions. So her left wings carry the same pattern as her right wings, flipped over. A leaf grows two halves, one on each side of the middle vein. Your body grew its left side and right side together too, from one tiny cell. One pattern, made twice, gives many living beings their shape.

teachings.teaching: Long and short shape each other. High and low lean on each other. Front and back follow each other.
teachings.link: Left and right go together in the same way. A left half is a half only because a right half goes with it. Together they make one butterfly.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4, the story of the blind men and the elephant (Jain teachers tell the story too)
teachings.teaching: Some men who could not see each touched one part of an elephant. The one who felt her head said an elephant is like a pot. The one who felt her ear said a winnowing basket. The one who felt her leg said a post. Each knew only a part, and they argued.
teachings.link: An elephant's trunk cannot tell you about her tail, because her front and back are different. But a butterfly's left side really does tell you her right side, because the two halves match. Even then, half the outside cannot tell you what is inside, like a heart sitting a little to the left.

science.text: Most animals, including humans, have a left side and a right side that nearly match. Scientists call this bilateral symmetry. It is common in animals that move forward, head first.
Bees can learn to tell a symmetric pattern from an uneven one, and many people find symmetric faces pleasing. Why living beings notice symmetry is still argued about.

other_view.view: The matching halves come from genes and growth alone. On this view, the symmetry of a butterfly is a pattern that we notice when we look, and nothing more.

practice.title: Two sides, one breath
practice.say: Sit up straight on the floor. Put one hand flat on each side of your chest. Breathe in slowly through your nose. Feel both hands rise together. Breathe out slowly. Feel both hands fall together. Let's do it five times. Now close your eyes and breathe once more. Do both sides move the same, or does one side move a little more?
practice.kid: Sit up straight. Put a hand on each side of your chest. Breathe in slowly. Both hands rise. Breathe out. Both hands fall. Do it five times.

ask: If you saw only your left half in a mirror, would you know what your right half looks like?
A butterfly's two sides match. Is she one pattern made twice, or two patterns that agree?
When you breathed with a hand on each side of your chest, did both sides move the same?

how_we_found_out.story: Long ago, many people in Europe believed that small creatures, like caterpillars, flies and worms, grew out of mud or rotting food. In 1668, an Italian doctor, Francesco Redi, kept meat in jars. Flies laid eggs only on meat they could reach, and maggots came only from those eggs. A German girl named Maria Sibylla Merian looked for herself too. From the age of thirteen, she raised silkworms and other caterpillars and fed them leaves. She watched each caterpillar eat, grow and make a hard case around their body, called a chrysalis. Weeks later, a butterfly or moth came out. Merian painted every step: the egg, the caterpillar, the chrysalis and the grown butterfly, with matching wings on both sides. In 1679 she printed her first book about caterpillars. In 1699, she sailed to Suriname in South America with her daughter Dorothea to study insects there. Women could not study at universities then, but her careful paintings helped show that every butterfly grows from an egg laid by another butterfly.
how_we_found_out.who: Maria Sibylla Merian, a German painter who studied insects, and Francesco Redi, an Italian doctor
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Small creatures like caterpillars and flies grow out of mud or rotting food. Redi's jars and Merian's caterpillars showed that they hatch from eggs laid by their parents.
